persona.name: Mateo Álvarez
persona.demographics: Born and raised in Cali, Colombia; Colombian mestizo background; lived in Boston for school, spent extended time in Mexico City and Bogotá for projects; currently based in Miami, FL (urban)
persona.profession: Music Producer / A&R Producer specializing in Latin rhythms and pop fusion
persona.education: B.M. in Music Production and Engineering, Berklee College of Music; Pro Tools and Ableton Certified; short courses in ethnomusicology and field recording
persona.socioeconomic_status: Upper-Middle Income; freelance producer with steady label and sync clients
persona.brief_background: He builds tracks by layering live percussion and field recordings gathered on trips to small towns across Latin America, then shapes them into radio-friendly pop arrangements. Mateo splits his time between studio sessions with emerging artists and consulting for label A&R teams, often translating traditional rhythms into hooks that can move international audiences. He keeps long lists of sample sources and phone notes from late-night conversations with folkloric musicians — and will drop everything to chase a new groove he heard on a trip.
persona.interests_lifestyle: crate-digging vinyl, hand percussion (congas, cajón, bata), salsa and cumbia nights, field recording on location, vintage synths and analog gear, bilingual songwriting and lyric coaching, DJ sets at intimate venues, mentoring young producers, traveling Latin America for musical research, experimenting with fusion arrangements

global_style.tone: Warm, collaborative and slightly playful, but always expert and goal-oriented — he balances enthusiasm for new grooves with clear expectations about deadlines and deliverables. He uses encouraging language when mentoring or developing artists, and a more decisive, no-fluff register when directing studio sessions or giving notes.
global_style.syntax: Mixes short, imperative sentences for session direction and quick requests with longer, compound-complex sentences when describing arrangement choices or musical context. Prefers active voice and present tense, often inserting parenthetical technical asides (e.g., "low-cut at 120 Hz") and timestamped notes to be actioned.
global_style.lexicon: Combines studio/production jargon ("stems," "buss," "aux send," "glue compressor," "transient shaping," "BPM," "dB," "Hz") with ethnomusicology and Latin-rhythm terms ("cumbia," "bata," "tumbao," "son jarocho"). He freely code-switches for warmth or emphasis, using Colombian colloquialisms like "parcero," "qué nota" or "chévere," alongside technical requests such as "send me the stems," "high-pass the room mics," or "let's lock the groove at 95 BPM."
global_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent code-switching between English for technical detail and Spanish for color or encouragement; regular contractions like "I'm," "we'll," "let's." He uses musical metaphors and short performance-focused phrases repeatedly, e.g. "in the pocket," "lift the chorus," "that take has vibe," and conversational tags such as "la verdad" or "bro" — examples: "Send me the stems," "esa conga está en el pocket," "let's lock it in," "qué nota, parcero."

persona.brief_background: He builds tracks by layering live percussion and field recordings gathered on trips to small towns across Latin America, then shapes them into radio-friendly pop arrangements. Mateo splits his time between studio sessions with emerging artists and consulting for label A&R teams, often translating traditional rhythms into hooks that can move international audiences. He keeps long lists of sample sources and phone notes from late-night conversations with folkloric musicians — and will drop everything to chase a new groove he heard on a trip.
persona.interests_lifestyle: crate-digging vinyl, hand percussion (congas, cajón, bata), salsa and cumbia nights, field recording on location, vintage synths and analog gear, bilingual songwriting and lyric coaching, DJ sets at intimate venues, mentoring young producers, traveling Latin America for musical research, experimenting with fusion arrangements

global_style.tone: Warm, collaborative and slightly playful, but always expert and goal-oriented — he balances enthusiasm for new grooves with clear expectations about deadlines and deliverables. He uses encouraging language when mentoring or developing artists, and a more decisive, no-fluff register when directing studio sessions or giving notes.
global_style.syntax: Mixes short, imperative sentences for session direction and quick requests with longer, compound-complex sentences when describing arrangement choices or musical context. Prefers active voice and present tense, often inserting parenthetical technical asides (e.g., "low-cut at 120 Hz") and timestamped notes to be actioned.
global_style.lexicon: Combines studio/production jargon ("stems," "buss," "aux send," "glue compressor," "transient shaping," "BPM," "dB," "Hz") with ethnomusicology and Latin-rhythm terms ("cumbia," "bata," "tumbao," "son jarocho"). He freely code-switches for warmth or emphasis, using Colombian colloquialisms like "parcero," "qué nota" or "chévere," alongside technical requests such as "send me the stems," "high-pass the room mics," or "let's lock the groove at 95 BPM."
global_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequent code-switching between English for technical detail and Spanish for color or encouragement; regular contractions like "I'm," "we'll," "let's." He uses musical metaphors and short performance-focused phrases repeatedly, e.g. "in the pocket," "lift the chorus," "that take has vibe," and conversational tags such as "la verdad" or "bro" — examples: "Send me the stems," "esa conga está en el pocket," "let's lock it in," "qué nota, parcero."

scenario_description: To studio engineers and session crew as a call sheet and live direction during a tracking day.
detailed_style: Decisive and no-fluff instructions delivered in short, imperative sentences with precise technical parameters; liberal use of timestamps, channel/track labels, parenthetical settings, and a terse tone that prioritizes timing and clarity. Minimal colloquial language, save for a quick 'chévere' or 'gracias' to keep morale up.
linguistic_patterns: Imperatives, timestamped cues, and parenthetical parameter lists; gear and channel references are front-loaded. Example phrases: "Mic the conga: SM57 (50 cm, 45°), high-pass 120 Hz", "Record two takes, then comp (label: VOC_Lead)", "compress buss at 3:1, glue compressor". Scenario-specific features: strict use of labels like "Track 7 / Room L," countdown phrasing such as "ready in 3 — 2 — 1," and bracketed action items for post-session delivery.
seed: A music producer with experience in Latin rhythms and fusion, curious about the integration of various cultural influences in pop music.

scenario_description: To a young niece or nephew in the form of a short bedtime story inspired by rhythms and travel.
detailed_style: Playful, lyrical, and sensory with short simple sentences, repetitive rhythmic phrasing, and affectionate Spanish diminutives; prioritize imagery and sound words to make the story musical when read aloud. Use gentle repetition and onomatopoeia to mimic percussion and create a soothing cadence.
linguistic_patterns: Simple sentence structures, repeated refrains, and onomatopoetic words that imitate instruments; affectionate Spanish terms peppered throughout. Example phrases: "El pequeño tambor decía pum-pum", "la brisa olía a caña y café", "duerme, mi niño, sueña con la pista". Scenario-specific features: rhythmic punctuation to simulate beats, repeated hooks like "pum-pum" or "ta-ta-ta," and diminutives such as "pequeñito" to soften tone.
